Chapter 5: The Power of Financial Education—Why Schools Don’t Teach Money Skills.
Have you ever noticed how schools spend so much time teaching us algebra, history, and science, but hardly ever mention money? Most of us graduate knowing how to solve equations or recite historical facts... but when it comes to managing a budget, investing in stocks, or even starting a business, we’re left in the dark.
And that gap? It leaves a lot of people unprepared for real life. Just think about it: the boy in our story saw this up close. His own father, who was highly educated and had a wall full of degrees, still struggled with his finances. He knew how to earn a paycheck, sure, but making money actually work for him? That was a whole different story.
On the other hand, his friend’s dad—someone with less formal schooling—seemed to have cracked the code on building wealth. That contrast really makes you wonder, doesn’t it? Why do schools skip over money skills?
Turns out, it’s mostly about tradition. Our school system was built for a world where stable jobs and pensions were the norm. But today, job security isn’t what it used to be. If you rely only on a steady paycheck, you might find yourself caught off guard by layoffs, sudden economic changes, or those surprise expenses life loves to throw at us.
The friend’s father believed the most important skill anyone can learn is how money actually works. He encouraged the boys to read books, attend seminars, and find mentors who could help them grow. He always said, “Financial education isn’t just a subject you study once. It’s a lifelong journey.” The world of money keeps changing, and if you stop learning, you’ll get left behind.
But here’s something to really pay attention to: knowledge alone isn’t enough. It’s one thing to read about investing or starting a business, but real understanding comes from actually doing it—buying that first stock, launching a small business, or negotiating a deal. Yeah, you’ll make mistakes. But every mistake is a lesson you just can’t get from a textbook.
Over time, the boy realized that financial education isn’t just about crunching numbers. It’s about your mindset, your daily habits, and the drive to keep learning. When you take responsibility for your own education, you start to spot opportunities where others just see problems. You become more resilient, more adaptable—and you discover that your life doesn’t have to be limited by fear or by what everyone else is doing.
